statements.text: AI is already causing net job losses in some industries.
statements.whyItMatters: Understanding current job displacement helps workers and policymakers prepare for ongoing changes.

statements.text: AI has not significantly changed overall employment levels yet.
statements.whyItMatters: This view suggests that the full impact of AI on jobs may still be years away.

statements.text: AI will lead to massive job displacement in the next decade.
statements.whyItMatters: This projection is critical for long-term workforce planning and education strategies.

statements.text: AI will create more jobs than it destroys over time.
statements.whyItMatters: This optimistic view informs policies that encourage AI adoption and innovation.

statements.text: Young workers are more likely to lose jobs due to AI.
statements.whyItMatters: This highlights the need for targeted support and retraining for younger generations.

statements.text: Low-skilled workers are most vulnerable to AI-driven job loss.

statements.text: Reskilling programs can help workers adapt to AI-driven changes.

statements.whyItMatters: This shows how regulation and planning can shape the future of work in a more equitable way.

consensusClaims.statement: AI has not significantly changed overall employment levels yet.

citations.quote: With recent New York Federal Reserve Bank research showing that computer science majors now have more trouble finding jobs than humanities majors, the risk of misleading students with false curriculum certainties is genuine.

In a sweeping global study, the National Bureau of Economic Research found that AI has had little to no impact on employment or productivity in almost 90% of firms over the past three years, based on responses from nearly 6,000 C-suite executives.
But BCG found that software engineering headcount across all ages in the technology sector has slowed but still grown, albeit at a much slower annual rate of 2% since the public release of ChatGPT.
Given all this noise, the average firm has chosen not to lay off workers on a large scale. Instead, many are silently closing the door to new ones.

The number of skills required for roles prone to automation are shrinking, the researchers found. They registered 7% fewer of those skills in job postings and also fewer skills emerging in these occupations.

The researchers note that the study focuses on the short-term impact of generative AI on the US labor market, so the effects on other regions or long-term impacts “remain uncertain as adoption scales.”
On the whole, there is a mildly negative correlation between employment trends and AI usage, suggesting that AI may be depressing job growth.

All in all, we find little association between various measures of AI intensity and job growth outside of selected tech industries, and conclude that so far AI has not been a major driver of the composition of employment gains, except perhaps in tech.

consensusClaims.statement: Office and administrative jobs are being replaced by AI at a high rate.

citations.quote: After the public launch of ChatGPT in November 2022, job postings for occupations that involve lots of structured and repetitive tasks, likely replaceable by generative AI, decreased by 13%.
6.1 million workers, primarily in clerical and administrative roles, lack adaptive capacity due to limited savings, advanced age, scarce local opportunities, and/or narrow skill sets.
Door-to-door sales workers and news and street vendors show the least adaptive capacity among the occupations in the top quartile of AI exposure.
In addition, job growth across several white-collar sectors has been tepid, pointing to AI’s growing role in the workforce.

contradictedClaims.statement: AI will create more jobs than it destroys over time.

citations.quote: Meanwhile, employer demand for jobs that require more analytical, technical, or creative work—potentially enhanced by artificial intelligence—grew 20%, according to a working paper coauthored by Harvard Business School Professor Suraj Srinivasan.

“Rather than solely eliminating jobs, generative AI creates new demand in augmentation-prone roles, suggesting that human-AI collaboration is a key driver of labor market transformation,” says Srinivasan.

AI is impacting the labor market by automating routine tasks, displacing some traditional roles, and simultaneously creating unprecedented demand for new positions in data science, AI ethics, and automation oversight.
The World Economic Forum projects 170 million new jobs will emerge by 2030, while 92 million will be displaced, equaling a net gain of 78 million positions.
Gartner predicts AI's impact on global jobs will be neutral through 2026.
Verizon CEO Dan Schulman has bluntly predicted that AI will cause unemployment to rise by up to 30% in the next two to five years.
The Boston Consulting Group (BCG) issued a clear-eyed report suggesting that 10%-15% of existing jobs could be eliminated as soon as 2031.

the analysis here shows that the workers with the highest AI exposure rates possess characteristics that give them higher capacity to navigate job transitions successfully—finding new employment quickly and minimizing earnings losses after job displacement.

Moreover, if AI fundamentally transforms the economy on a scale comparable to the industrial revolution (as some experts have suggested could be possible), it could make entire skill sets redundant across several occupations simultaneously.

In doing so, it makes clear the existence of both large zones of strong resilience to job loss across the workforce as well as concentrated pockets of heightened vulnerability if displacement were to occur.
Policymakers concerned about AI’s job displacement potential may wish to focus attention on workers with the weakest adaptive capacity, who are likely to face the highest welfare costs if displaced.
